task_brief: This is day 6 of "Pictures, Sounds, and Simple Data". That is unit 5 in grade 3. Today is a correction and reflection about checking if a fact seems true. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Collect a small set of data and create a simple picture graph with a short conclusion. Today helps by working on checking if a fact seems true. Your unit also covers sorting and counting objects, simple picture graphs, choosing a picture that fits, and comparing two data sets. Today adds real evidence toward your unit project.
primary_task: Look back at your earlier work on checking if a fact seems true and fix it. Make a fix-it list. For each mistake write four things: what went wrong, why it went wrong, what you changed, and how you know it works now. Include one thing that failed before and works now. Then look at all your mistakes together. What do they have in common? Name one habit that would catch it sooner. Everything you need is printed in activity_setup. It has the exact case, what should happen, how to try it, checks, and a paper choice worth the same score. Do not wait for another handout or app. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about checking if a fact seems true. It is part of "Pictures, Sounds, and Simple Data". Later days in this unit cover other things, like sorting and counting objects. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about checking if a fact seems true; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 3 you need one clear try with a grown-up nearby. Say or write your reason in a sentence or two. Drawings, objects, or spoken answers are all fine.

concept_teaching.title: Pause, minimize, verify, and document: checking if a fact seems true
concept_teaching.entry_check: Before reading, write one prediction about checking if a fact seems true and one observation that could show the prediction is wrong. This readiness record is no-penalty evidence.
explanation: checking if a fact seems true is about making a clear choice and showing why it works. First name what the result should do. Then point to the step, label, or fact that supports your choice.
A check is different from a guess. Write what you expect before you try it. Compare what happened with what you expected. If they differ, circle the first place they stop matching.
A fix needs a reason. Change one thing that your evidence supports, try the same checks again, and keep the old and new work. That record shows your thinking even when the first try was wrong.

Separate the stated purpose from the information or action requested, choose the least-exposing safe response, and record which printed detail supports the decision. You may use paper, objects, labelled drawings, or precise steps when a computer is not the best tool.

debugging_reasoning.title: Use the six-move evidence cycle
required_moves: Symptom: record expected versus actual without explaining it away.
Hypothesis: state one falsifiable cause about the claim or design state before revising.
Inspection: identify the first trace row or printed detail that bears on the hypothesis.
Predicted effect: state what one controlled change should alter and what it should leave unchanged.
Test and interpretation: compare actual with the prediction and mark the hypothesis supported, rejected, or not fully tested.
Verification: rerun all relevant checks and record any new limitation or next hypothesis.
debugging_reasoning.anti_guessing_rule: A working final artifact without a pre-change hypothesis and inspectable evidence is incomplete debugging/revision evidence.

remediation_routes.learner_signal: My conclusion names the topic but does not connect to exact printed evidence.
remediation_routes.title: Different representation: evidence cards and arrows
remediation_routes.alternate_teaching: Copy each printed fact onto a separate card. Draw an arrow from a fact to a claim only when the fact would make that claim more or less credible. Unconnected claims must be revised or removed.
remediation_routes.analogue_task: Use four new cards about a fictional library sign to build a fact → claim → check map for checking if a fact seems true; do not use the protected case.
remediation_routes.return_check: Complete the fresh mastery check with teaching materials closed. The original protected solution remains withheld.

remediation_routes.learner_signal: I changed or chose something before recording the mismatch and a testable reason.
remediation_routes.title: Different routine: the six-box evidence ladder
remediation_routes.alternate_teaching: Use six boxes in order: expected/actual, first divergence or decisive detail, hypothesis, predicted effect, one revision, rerun interpretation. Do not enter the revision box until the first four constrain what the change is meant to test.
remediation_routes.analogue_task: Apply the six boxes to a separate fictional clock-card mismatch related to checking if a fact seems true. Stop after the prediction, explain what result would reject the hypothesis, then finish the check.
remediation_routes.return_check: Complete the fresh mastery check independently. A correct but low-confidence response receives confirmation tied to evidence, not automatic reteaching.

Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. remediation: Reteaching for checking if a fact seems true follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for checking if a fact seems true, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for checking if a fact seems true works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of checking if a fact seems true, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking checking if a fact seems true mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply checking if a fact seems true under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on checking if a fact seems true rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
